findings.issue_text: [BUG] `organization_context` is defined nowhere in this endpoint or its imports, so the expression `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError on every audit-logs request from a non-superuser (the `or` only short-circuits for superusers). Every GET of /api/0/organizations/<slug>/auditlogs/ by a normal org admin or member evaluates enable_advanced unconditionally, hits the undefined name, and returns a 500 — the audit log UI and API are down for all non-superuser users of every organization.

[BUG] The buffer switches its Redis data structure from SET (SADD/SCARD/SUNIONSTORE/SSCAN) to ZSET (ZADD/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZSCAN) with no data migration, so every `span-buf:s:*` key already written as a SET by the old code makes the new p.zadd (buffer.py:197), the zunionstore/zcard calls in add-buffer.lua (lines 46-53), and the flusher's p.zscan (buffer.py:434) fail with WRONGTYPE. During a rolling deploy of the spans process consumer and (separately deployed) flusher, each buffered key created pre-deploy causes a redis ResponseError WRONGTYPE: the consumer's pipeline raises and retries the same batch into the same error, and the flusher cannot scan those segments — spans buffered at deploy time are unprocessable until their TTL expires, and old-version processes hit the mirror-image error on keys the new code already converted.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil to the raw value of self.key, which for the only caller (audit logs, order_by="-datetime") is a Python datetime object, and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. A superuser calling the audit-logs endpoint with optimized_pagination=true on any organization holding at least one AuditLogEntry gets a TypeError 500 out of build_cursor's key() call instead of a paginated response — the optimized path cannot ever succeed.

[BUG] The advanced negative-offset branch slices the queryset as queryset[negative:stop], and Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ raises ValueError ("Negative indexing is not supported in querysets") for negative slice bounds — the comment's justification that "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually false. Whenever the feature is actually exercised (enable_advanced_features=True plus a negative-offset cursor — both client-controllable, since the cursor format is public base64 and the gate is a raw query param), get_result raises and the request 500s; the documented feature has no working execution path.

[BUG] process_batch hard-indexes val["end_timestamp_precise"], so any span message whose payload lacks the field raises KeyError inside the batch loop. One such message makes process_batch raise, failing the entire Kafka batch — all spans in that batch stop being processed and the consumer retries into the same error; if the field is present but null, None flows in as a zadd score, which redis-py rejects with DataError.

[BUG] The eviction only executes inside this script (invoked at root-span arrival), while process_spans zadds straggler spans directly into the same `span-buf:s:` segment key (buffer.py:197) with no eviction, and the diff deletes the flusher-side `max_segment_spans` guard that was the only cap on total span count at flush time — so the 1000-span bound is not enforced for spans arriving after root arrival. Segments whose children straggle in after the root's script run can still exceed 1000 spans at flush time (bounded only by max_segment_bytes), so oversized segments are emitted with no span-count check and no metric, defeating the eviction's stated purpose.

[ADVISORY] The eviction drops spans silently: the removed buffer.py guard emitted metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded") and a logger.error on over-limit segments, but zpopmin truncates with no counter, log, or signal of any kind. When production traces exceed 1000 spans, the oldest spans are silently removed from the segment and on-call has no way to detect the data loss — existing dashboards and alarms keyed on segment_span_count_exceeded go dark exactly when truncation starts.

[ADVISORY] The diff's headline behavior — the set→zset migration, zunionstore merging, and the 1000-span eviction — has no test anywhere in the diff; the only test changes add end_timestamp_precise plumbing values to existing fixtures. An off-by-one in `span_count - 1000`, a WRONGTYPE from the type migration, or a zpopmin ordering bug ships undetected; the next engineer touching the eviction has no executable specification of the intended bound or truncation semantics to verify against.

[ADVISORY] The entire pagination half of this diff — the optimized_pagination query param, OptimizedCursorPaginator, and negative-offset support — is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction), has no calling client in the tree, and is gated only on an undocumented raw query parameter with no feature flag or options entry. A customer-facing endpoint (audit logs) gains three crash surfaces (the NameError, the datetime TypeError, the negative-slice ValueError) that ride along with a spans PR, and the new behavior cannot be disabled without a code deploy because there is no flag to flip.

[ADVISORY] This hunk deletes the only reader of self.max_segment_spans and the replacement cap (1000) is hardcoded as an opaque constant inside the Lua script, leaving the still-registered option dead. Operators tuning the spans-buffer max_segment_spans setting (self-hosted configs, SRE dynamic settings) get no effect, and the effective segment-size bound now lives in two independent places — Python options and the embedded Lua constant — that will drift on the next change.

[ADVISORY] Negative-offset "support" is speculative generality: nothing in the codebase produces negative cursor offsets (build_cursor only emits non-negative ones), so the max(0, offset) clamp only alters behavior for forged cursors, and the accompanying comments here and in cursors.py:26-27 assert a capability (bidirectional negative-offset pagination) that the Django ORM in fact rejects. Deleting the clamp, the OptimizedCursorPaginator advanced branch, and the cursors.py comments removes three places-to-maintain with no behavior change for any legitimate client; keeping them guarantees future maintainers spend effort on a path only forged input can reach and that crashes when reached.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates OffsetPaginator.get_result's boundary logic (~35 lines: offset/extra computation, prev-cursor trimming, reversal, build_cursor invocation) nearly verbatim instead of subclassing the existing paginator. Any future fix to cursor boundary handling (a recurring bug class in this file) must now be applied to two copies; when one copy is missed, audit-logs pagination silently behaves differently from every other offset-paginated endpoint in the codebase.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-following bound is cut from 10000 to 1000 iterations and the comment documenting the correctness envelope ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") is deleted with no replacement note, metric, or stated reason. Segment trees with redirect chains deeper than 1000 hops now fall out of the loop with a stale set_span_id, so their spans are grouped under the wrong set key and emit split or incorrect segments, with no error or counter to notice the boundary changed by 10x.

[BUG] The endpoint computes `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` unconditionally on every request, but `organization_context` is never defined anywhere in this method (the diff introduces the reference with no definition and the pre-existing get() has no such local). Every GET to /api/0/organizations/<org>/auditlogs/ raises NameError and returns 500 for all users — not only those passing optimized_pagination — breaking audit-log access org-wide, and it happens before the flag check so even default requests fail.

[BUG] The script switches span-buf:s:* keys from SET to ZSET operations (zcard/zunionstore/zpopmin) with no type check, no migration, and no flush of in-flight data, so any key written as a plain SET by the pre-deploy version (TTL up to set_timeout) hits a WRONGTYPE error on every zcard/zunionstore call. During the rolling deploy, every span arriving whose parent set or merged set was written by old code fails the whole eval, the span consumer errors and retries those messages until the legacy keys expire, and old-version workers sadd-ing onto keys the new version converted to ZSETs fail symmetrically — a span-ingestion outage for the entire TTL window.

[BUG] _load_segment_data now issues zscan against span-buf:s:* keys that the pre-deploy version wrote as plain SETs, with no migration or type-tolerant handling anywhere in the diff, so the flush path hits WRONGTYPE on legacy in-flight segments. Immediately after deploy the flush job crashes on every pre-existing segment key and retries in a loop, blocking segment flushing for all traces until the old keys expire past set_timeout.

[BUG] process_batch indexes val["end_timestamp_precise"] directly with no fallback, while every sibling field on the next lines is read with val.get() because the ingest_spans_v1 payload does not guarantee presence, so any message from an older producer or without a precise timestamp raises KeyError. The KeyError fails the entire process_batch, so the Kafka consumer retries the same poison message indefinitely and stalls that partition's span ingestion; a null value instead flows into the redis zadd pipeline as a None score, which the pipeline rejects.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator but calls CursorPaginator-only machinery — self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev) in get_result and self._is_asc in get_item_key — none of which exists on BasePaginator, so the class is broken against the base it declares. The optimized audit-log path raises AttributeError before any query runs, so any administrator invoking optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 rather than a page — the new admin surface never works at all.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key computes int(math.floor(value)) on getattr(item, self.key), but its only in-diff caller passes order_by="-datetime", so value is a datetime object — exactly the case DateTimePaginator exists to convert, which this class ignores. Building any cursor from AuditLogEntry rows raises TypeError (cannot floor a datetime), so the optimized pagination path 500s on the first page instead of returning rows to the admin who enabled it.

[BUG] The enable_advanced_features branch slices queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset on the asserted grounds that "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically", which is false — Django querysets reject negative slice bounds. Any admin presenting a negative-offset cursor on the optimized audit-log path gets a Django 'Negative indexing is not supported' AssertionError (500) instead of a page; the in-code comment is the only verification this branch ever received.

[BUG] The shared BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative offsets only on the non-prev branch (max(0, offset)) while prev cursors keep the raw negative offset, so the "bidirectional negative-offset pagination" that the comment and the new cursors.py comment advertise is implemented on one branch only — and unlike the OptimizedCursorPaginator, this base change is not gated by enable_advanced_features at all, so every existing offset paginator inherits the half-feature. A prev cursor carrying a negative offset — which the diff now documents as supported — slices queryset[-N:...] and raises Django's negative-indexing error (500) on DB-backed endpoints, while the same negative offset on a next cursor silently rewinds to offset 0 and returns page 1, so API clients get either 500s or silently wrong pages depending on direction.

[BUG] The endpoint swaps paginator_cls per request based on the raw optimized_pagination query param, but DateTimePaginator and OptimizedCursorPaginator produce and consume incompatible cursor encodings (DateTimePaginator converts datetime values; OptimizedCursorPaginator.value_from_cursor returns the raw cursor value and floors item keys to ints), and nothing in the diff defines cursor interchange between the two. A client that pages with the param unset and then replays the returned cursor with the param set (or vice versa) sends a cursor the other paginator cannot decode — the raw value feeds datetime filters and raises ValidationError/500 or selects the wrong time window — so admins get broken or empty pages mid-stream with no error contract defined.

[BUG] The max_segment_spans flush guard (and its segment_span_count_exceeded metric) was deleted on the assumption that the Lua zpopmin caps every set at 1000, but the Python-side merge path at buffer.py:197-198 zadds into the same span-buf:s:* keyspace with no eviction, so the assumption does not hold for segments assembled through the pipeline. Segments written via the Python merge path (or finalized before any Lua invocation touches that key) exceed the old cap and now flush downstream unbounded, and the metric that previously made oversized segments observable is gone — operators lose both the guard and the signal in one change.

[ADVISORY] The eviction cap is a hardcoded 1000 in Lua while the Python side's configurable self.max_segment_spans just had its only enforcement deleted from _load_segment_data, leaving the option with no reader anywhere in the diff. Operators tuning the max-segment-spans option see zero effect (the knob ships inert), and the effective cap silently diverges from whatever is configured — the limit now lives as a magic constant that cannot be changed at deploy time without editing the Lua script.

[ADVISORY] Eviction via zpopmin drops the oldest-end_timestamp spans with no metric, log, or stated acceptance criterion for which spans must survive — unlike every other drop path in the buffer, which increments a metric (segment_size_exceeded, segment_span_count_exceeded). Once a set reaches 1000, late-arriving spans — the norm for out-of-order tracing delivery and for Kafka redelivery after rebalance — are inserted and immediately evicted as the new minimum, so high-volume traces systematically lose their late spans and operators have no signal to detect the truncation.

[ADVISORY] The PR's headline behavior — eviction during insert — has no verification: every test change in the diff (test_buffer.py, test_flusher.py, test_consumer.py) only adds end_timestamp_precise to fixtures, and no test constructs a >1000-span set, asserts which spans survive zpopmin, or asserts that an oversized segment now flushes instead of being skipped. The deleted segment_span_count_exceeded guard and the new eviction path ship with no acceptance criterion; a regression in eviction (wrong victims, off-by-one in span_count - 1000, evicting spans the segment still needs) silently truncates every high-volume segment and no CI run can catch it.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds ~90 lines of new pagination behavior — the OptimizedCursorPaginator class, the base-class negative-offset change at paginator.py:182-184, and the query-param-gated audit-log path — with zero tests: no test file for api/paginator.py or organization_auditlogs.py appears in the diff, and the only test changes are span-consumer fixtures. Always-broken paths like the missing build_queryset/_is_asc helpers and the datetime floor ship undetected to an admin-facing endpoint, and the shared BasePaginator.get_result change — inherited by every offset-paginated endpoint in the API — is validated by nothing before it affects all of them.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-loop bound is cut from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting that this limit is what determines whether deep segment trees join correctly is deleted. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 now exit the loop without joining (silent segment loss for pathological traces), and the next reader has no documentation of why 1000 is correct or what breaks above it — the stated invariant was simply dropped.

[ADVISORY] Both zunionstore calls use the default SUM aggregation, so a payload present in both source keys — the at-least-once redelivery case the buffer already models in test_flush_rebalance re-adds a span to span_key while it already sits in set_key — gets its timestamp scores summed instead of deduplicated as the old sunionstore did. The corrupted score (roughly double the timestamp) reorders the zset, so zpopmin later evicts the wrong spans and score-dependent ordering behaves unpredictably in exactly the rebalance scenario the buffer is designed to survive.

[BUG] This diff grafts an unrelated admin-gated 'optimized pagination' feature onto the audit-log endpoint — not traceable to the PR's stated intent (spans buffer eviction) — and its flag expression unconditionally evaluates `organization_context.member.has_global_access` on every GET although `organization_context` is not defined anywhere in this method or module. Every non-superuser request to the organization audit-logs endpoint raises NameError and returns a 500 even when the `optimized_pagination` query param is absent (the `enable_advanced` line runs before the `if`), taking the endpoint down org-wide; the feature itself is a raw query-param opt-in with no feature flag and no requirement behind it.

[BUG] Deleting the `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` check in `_load_segment_data` removes the only enforcement of the segment span-count cap, and the replacement insert-time eviction exists only in add-buffer.lua, so segments written through `SpansBuffer.process_spans` (the `p.zadd(set_key, ...)` at line ~197 into the same `span-buf:s:*` keys) remain uncapped. A segment built via the process-consumer path with more than max_segment_spans spans is now flushed downstream with no cap anywhere — the invariant this PR claims to move from flush-time to insert-time is not enforced on one of its two insertion paths — and the `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` metric/error alert disappears with it, so operators lose both the guard and the signal.

[BUG] The rewrite of the shared OffsetPaginator.get_result (the base of DateTimePaginator, used by dozens of existing endpoints) to deliberately pass through negative offsets for prev-cursors is untraceable to the spans-buffer intent and rests on the false premise that 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' — Django ORM queryset slicing raises on negative bounds. Any OffsetPaginator/DateTimePaginator endpoint handed a prev-cursor with a negative offset now issues `queryset[-N:...]` and fails with 'Negative indexing is not supported' (500), while the new `max(0, offset)` clamp for non-prev cursors converts previously-erroring negative offsets into silently wrong page-0 results — a behavior change on a hot shared code path that no requirement in this PR calls for.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~90 lines of the existing cursor-paginator get_result logic with its sole caller being the unrelated audit-log branch added in the same diff, and it has already drifted: the prev-dedup branch compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` against the raw offset while the slice used `start_offset`. Maintainers of paginator.py now own two near-identical cursor implementations to keep in sync (the drift means a negative-offset prev page serves a duplicated boundary row to any admin using the smuggled param); deleting this class together with the audit-log branch removes ~130 lines across two files with zero loss to the stated spans-buffer intent.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises the eviction behavior this PR exists to deliver — every updated fixture buffers at most 5 spans, so the `span_count > 1000` → `zpopmin` path in add-buffer.lua runs only in production. A regression in the eviction arithmetic (popping the full span_count instead of span_count - 1000, or the `span_count == 0` zcard fallback at lines 53-55 never firing) ships silently and either defeats the cap entirely — recreating the unbounded buffer growth the PR claims to fix — or over-evicts and silently drops spans; both failures stay invisible until Redis memory or segment completeness breaks.

[ADVISORY] The new insert-time cap is the magic number 1000 hardcoded in Lua while the Python-side `self.max_segment_spans`, whose only consumer this diff deletes, is left in place, so the enforced cap has no single source of truth. An operator who raises or lowers the Python-side max_segment_spans setting gets no effect anywhere (dead configuration after this PR), and if its configured value differs from 1000 the shipped eviction cap silently disagrees with the documented segment-size limit.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-chain loop bound is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with its explanatory comment ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined correctly') deleted — a change unrelated to eviction that weakens a documented join guarantee. Traces whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 hops — which the old bound explicitly promised to follow — now terminate mid-chain and the span is hset to an intermediate segment id, splitting segments that previously joined correctly, with no test or flag covering the new bound.

[BUG] _load_segment_data unpacks ZSCAN results as (member, score) pairs (`for span, _ in zscan_values`), but redis-py parses ZSCAN into a (cursor, {member: score}) dict, so iterating yields the payload bytes themselves and the two-name unpack raises ValueError. Every flush of every non-empty segment raises ValueError at the `sizes[key] += sum(len(span) for span, _ in zscan_values)` line before any data is returned, so no buffered segment can ever be published — segments accumulate in Redis until `set_timeout` expires them and all buffered span data is silently lost.

[BUG] The script flips the shared `span-buf:s:*` key space from SETs to ZSETs (zcard/zunionstore here, zadd at buffer.py:197, zscan at buffer.py:434) with no key versioning or migration, while old consumer instances still SADD into the exact same keys during a rolling deploy. During any rolling deploy, new-version zcard/zunionstore/zadd/zscan against keys holding old-version SADD data (and old-version sadd against new ZSET keys) fail with WRONGTYPE, so segments buffered before the deploy can never be merged or flushed and their spans are lost when the TTL expires.

[BUG] process_batch reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct indexing while every neighboring field uses `.get()`, because the ingest-spans schema permits spans without (or with null) precise end timestamps, e.g. from older Relay/producer versions. A span lacking the field raises KeyError inside process_batch (or feeds a None score into zadd at buffer.py:198, which redis rejects), poisoning and repeatedly failing the Kafka batch — the consumer stalls on spans the pre-diff code processed fine.

[BUG] `enable_advanced` references `organization_context`, which is not defined anywhere in this endpoint's get() (not imported, not assigned in this method), and the expression evaluates unconditionally on every request rather than only when optimized_pagination=true is passed. Every non-superuser request to GET /api/0/organizations/<slug>/auditlogs/ raises NameError and returns a 500 (superusers short-circuit on is_superuser), taking down the audit-logs endpoint for all regular organization admins regardless of the query parameter.

[BUG] The advanced branch slices the queryset with a negative bound (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), but Django querysets do not support negative slice bounds — slicing compiles to SQL OFFSET, which raises — so the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any superuser who enables `optimized_pagination=true` with a cursor carrying a negative offset gets a 500: the sole advertised capability of OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot execute, and the promised 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' is unreachable in any deployment.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a collage of DateTimePaginator method bodies (get_item_key, value_from_cursor, and the self.build_queryset call) grafted onto BasePaginator, which does not define build_queryset — BasePaginator's own get_result is pure offset slicing with no value-filtered queryset building — and its value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value where a datetime is required. The first request through the optimized path raises AttributeError ('OptimizedCursorPaginator' object has no attribute 'build_queryset') before any query runs, so admins who set optimized_pagination=true get a 500 on every request and the feature is dead on arrival.

[ADVISORY] The endpoint forks into a second, parallel pagination implementation (OptimizedCursorPaginator, ~90 duplicated lines stitched from OffsetPaginator and DateTimePaginator) selected by an undocumented magic query-param string comparison (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus a role check, with no feature flag or options entry and no tests in the diff. One endpoint now serves two divergence-prone pagination contracts whose behavior differs by caller role; operators cannot disable the new path without a code deploy; and the duplicated paginator will drift from BasePaginator fixes, with breakage surfacing only as confusing admin-only 500s that non-admin reproduction cannot hit.

[ADVISORY] The eviction path silently truncates segments — zpopmin discards the oldest spans and publishes a partial segment with no metric or log — while this same PR deletes the flusher's only loud signal (the segment_span_count_exceeded metric and skip in buffer.py:446-452), so oversized segments now ship silently instead of failing observably. Operators lose the only means of detecting truncation; traces with >1000 spans are persisted as segments missing their earliest spans, so downstream segment processing computes from partial data; and when the root span's end_timestamp ranks among the oldest (clock skew / out-of-order ingestion), the has_root_span marker still fires and a rootless segment is published.

[ADVISORY] The 1000-span cap is enforced only on the Lua insert path; process_spans writes into the same `span-buf:s:{...}` keys via `p.zadd` with no cap or eviction, and the flusher-side count guard was deleted, so the advertised bound is not a real invariant. Segments assembled through the Python tree path grow without limit in Redis (memory pressure on the shared cluster for hot traces) and exceed the intended cap with no remaining code path — insert-time or flush-time — able to notice or bound them.

[ADVISORY] The eviction threshold is a hardcoded bare `1000` that replaces the existing configurable `self.max_segment_spans` — whose only reader this diff deletes from buffer.py — and the script now holds two same-valued `1000` literals with different units (redirect depth at line 30 vs span count here). Operators who configured max_segment_spans get silently ignored values (the option is now dead config), and the next editor can conflate the depth-1000 with the count-1000 or change one without the other, with no named constant tying the Lua cap to the Python option.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-walk bound is silently lowered from 10001 to 1001 iterations while the comment documenting the tradeoff ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') is deleted. Redirect chains between 1001 and 10000 deep now fall out of the loop with set_span_id pointing at a mid-chain node, so the following hset buffers subsequent spans under the wrong set id and the segment fragments never join — those fragments expire via TTL and their spans are lost, with the deleted comment hiding the known limitation.

[ADVISORY] The shared offset paginator's negative-offset handling is now internally inconsistent and contradicts its own comment: forward cursors silently clamp negative offsets to 0 (returning page one), while prev cursors pass the unclamped negative offset straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which raises. Every endpoint using this base paginator now accepts forged/corrupted cursors with negative offsets either silently — returning the first page as if it were valid and masking cursor corruption — or with a 500 on the is_prev branch, instead of uniformly rejecting them as the pre-diff code did.

[BUG] This audit-log pagination feature (hidden `optimized_pagination` query param, superuser/global-access gating, and the new OptimizedCursorPaginator) is an objective change unrelated to the PR's stated intent ('Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'), smuggled into a Redis spans-buffer PR without acceptance from anyone reviewing audit-log API behavior. Role-dependent pagination semantics and a new undocumented query parameter with no feature flag or options entry ship under a PR whose reviewers accepted only span-buffer changes; regressions in this security-sensitive endpoint are unowned, cannot be disabled without a code revert, and cursor tokens minted by the admin-only paginator are fed back to DateTimePaginator when the param is dropped or the link is opened by a non-admin, breaking pagination continuity for audit-log users.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the queryset with a negative start (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` where `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), which raises Django's `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, directly contradicting the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any superuser/global-access request to the audit-logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a client-crafted cursor carrying a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses ints without rejecting negatives, as the cursors.py comment in this diff confirms) returns a 500 from an uncaught AssertionError instead of the promised bidirectional pagination; the unclamped prev-cursor else-branch at line 881 crashes the same way.

[BUG] _load_segment_data now issues `p.zscan` against `span-buf:s:*` keys, but this diff changes those keys' Redis type from set to zset with no migration, so every key written by pre-deploy code (sadd/sunionstore) is still a SET with live TTL when the new flusher first runs. The first post-deploy flush cycle raises Redis WRONGTYPE on every still-live pre-deploy segment key, crashing the flush batch; retries keep failing until the TTL expires, so all segments buffered across the deploy window are silently lost.

[BUG] The script switches span-buf:s:* keys from set operations (scard/sunionstore) to zset operations (zcard/zunionstore) while buffer.py process_spans switches sadd to zadd on the same key names, with no key versioning, so old- and new-code consumers coexisting during a rolling deploy operate on the same keys with incompatible Redis types. During the deploy window every cross-version touch raises WRONGTYPE — old Lua `scard` on a zset written by new Python zadd, new Lua `zcard` on a set written by old code — so span insertion script calls error and incoming spans are dropped for the duration of mixed-version operation.

[BUG] The new eviction (`zpopmin` of the lowest end_timestamp_precise members whenever count > 1000) silently deletes spans that were accepted into the buffer — including segments well under the accepted max_segment_bytes budget — and the flusher then emits the remaining spans as a complete segment because has_root_span, the only completeness gate, is unaffected. Flushed segments are silently missing their earliest-ending spans with no marker, metric, or structural signal, so downstream segment assembly and trace views show truncated data indistinguishable from a complete segment — the buffer's accepted contract (skip oversized segments whole and loudly) is replaced by unmarked partial emission that no review accepted.

[BUG] process_batch direct-indexes `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with no `.get` fallback for a field this diff itself introduces to the wire contract (the consumer test fixture adds the field only in this PR), making the consumer incompatible with in-flight messages produced by pre-deploy producers. During a rolling deploy, any Kafka message lacking the field raises KeyError inside process_batch, fails the batch, and turns the message into a poison pill the consumer retries indefinitely, stalling span ingestion on that partition.

[ADVISORY] The eviction path drops buffered spans with no metrics.incr or logger call, breaking the buffer's established observability contract where every drop path (segment_size_exceeded, segment_span_count_exceeded) is instrumented. On-call engineers investigating incomplete segments or Redis memory pressure cannot distinguish evicted spans from lost ingestion, and the spans.buffer.flush_segments dashboards give no signal that the new dominant drop path ever fired.

[ADVISORY] Deleting the max_segment_spans check removes the only enforcement of the max_segment_spans option and the segment_span_count_exceeded metric, while the real cap becomes the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua that operators cannot configure. Operators who tune max_segment_spans now set a silently inert option — settings changes have no effect and the bound can only move via a Lua code deploy; monitoring and alerts keyed on segment_span_count_exceeded go permanently to zero.

[ADVISORY] The redirect-following bound drops from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the accepted tradeoff ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') is deleted, silently weakening a documented constraint with no stated justification. Traces whose redirect chains exceed depth 1000 — previously joined per the documented bound — now attach spans to an intermediate set, splitting the segment into multiple partial flushes with no error anywhere; whoever accepted the 10k bound was never asked to accept 1000.

[ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises the eviction logic (zpopmin count arithmetic, eviction direction by end_timestamp_precise, the span_count fallback) — every test change is a mechanical end_timestamp_precise field addition. A regression in the count expression or pop direction ships undetected and silently changes which buffered spans get dropped — e.g., popping newest instead of oldest would discard live spans while flushing stale ones.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates ~90 lines of the existing cursor-paginator get_result logic with its sole caller being the unrelated audit-log branch added in the same diff, and it has already drifted: the prev-dedup branch compares `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` against the raw offset while the slice used `start_offset`. Maintainers of paginator.py now own two near-identical cursor implementations to keep in sync (the drift means a negative-offset prev page serves a duplicated boundary row to any admin using the smuggled param); deleting this class together with the audit-log branch removes ~130 lines across two files with zero loss to the stated spans-buffer intent.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` that conditionally enables negative offsets (`if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:`) and then applies the existing “prev” de-dup/trimming logic unchanged: `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra:`. With a negative `offset`, `offset + limit + extra` can be <= 0, making this condition impossible to satisfy and breaking the boundary trimming behavior for that advanced negative-offset path. This is a concrete drift/incorrectness in the newly added code path, reachable via the new audit-log endpoint branch (`optimized_pagination=true` + `enable_advanced_features=True`). Additionally, the class is near-duplicate logic, increasing maintenance risk, but the negative-offset logic bug is directly evidenced in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] No test in the diff exercises the eviction behavior this PR exists to deliver — every updated fixture buffers at most 5 spans, so the `span_count > 1000` → `zpopmin` path in add-buffer.lua runs only in production. A regression in the eviction arithmetic (popping the full span_count instead of span_count - 1000, or the `span_count == 0` zcard fallback at lines 53-55 never firing) ships silently and either defeats the cap entirely — recreating the unbounded buffer growth the PR claims to fix — or over-evicts and silently drops spans; both failures stay invisible until Redis memory or segment completeness breaks.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new eviction logic in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` (`span_count` tracking, `zcard` fallback, and `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`). The updated/added tests in this diff only adjust fixtures to include `end_timestamp_precise` and still operate on very small span sets (a handful of spans per batch), so nothing in the shown test changes would exercise the new `span_count > 1000` eviction branch or the `span_count == 0` fallback. That’s a concrete, diff-grounded coverage gap for newly introduced nontrivial behavior, not a proven functional defect by itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new insert-time cap is the magic number 1000 hardcoded in Lua while the Python-side `self.max_segment_spans`, whose only consumer this diff deletes, is left in place, so the enforced cap has no single source of truth. An operator who raises or lowers the Python-side max_segment_spans setting gets no effect anywhere (dead configuration after this PR), and if its configured value differs from 1000 the shipped eviction cap silently disagrees with the documented segment-size limit.

adjudication.rationale: In `spans/buffer.py` the flush-time enforcement of `self.max_segment_spans` is removed: the block that checked `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and skipped oversized segments is deleted and replaced with simply extending payloads from `zscan_values`. Meanwhile, the Lua script `add-buffer.lua` introduces a hardcoded eviction threshold `if span_count > 1000 then ...` using `zpopmin`. This means the effective span-count cap is now always 1000 (at insert/merge time) regardless of the Python-side `max_segment_spans` value, so changing `max_segment_spans` would no longer affect behavior and can silently disagree with the enforced cap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-chain loop bound is silently reduced from 10000 to 1000 with its explanatory comment ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined correctly') deleted — a change unrelated to eviction that weakens a documented join guarantee. Traces whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 hops — which the old bound explicitly promised to follow — now terminate mid-chain and the span is hset to an intermediate segment id, splitting segments that previously joined correctly, with no test or flag covering the new bound.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` changes the redirect resolution loop from `for i = 0, 10000 do  -- theoretically this limit ...` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and removes the explanatory comment. That is a real, diff-grounded behavioral change: redirect chains longer than 1000 will stop earlier than before. The finding’s downstream impact (joining may split for >1000 hops) is plausible given the loop’s purpose (walking redirects to find `set_span_id`), but the diff alone can’t prove it occurs in practice or that 10k was a contractual guarantee. Still, silently reducing the bound without justification/tests/flag is a concrete review issue tied to the changed logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] _load_segment_data unpacks ZSCAN results as (member, score) pairs (`for span, _ in zscan_values`), but redis-py parses ZSCAN into a (cursor, {member: score}) dict, so iterating yields the payload bytes themselves and the two-name unpack raises ValueError. Every flush of every non-empty segment raises ValueError at the `sizes[key] += sum(len(span) for span, _ in zscan_values)` line before any data is returned, so no buffered segment can ever be published — segments accumulate in Redis until `set_timeout` expires them and all buffered span data is silently lost.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `sscan` to `zscan` and then treats the returned values as an iterable of `(member, score)` pairs (`for span, _ in zscan_values` and `sum(len(span) for span, _ in zscan_values)`). That matches redis-py’s typical `ZSCAN` return shape of `(cursor, [(member, score), ...])`, not a `(cursor, {member: score})` dict. The finding’s core claim (that redis-py parses ZSCAN into a dict, causing unpacking to raise `ValueError`) is not supported by what the diff shows and contradicts common `zscan` semantics; the described “every flush raises ValueError” cascade does not follow from the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The script flips the shared `span-buf:s:*` key space from SETs to ZSETs (zcard/zunionstore here, zadd at buffer.py:197, zscan at buffer.py:434) with no key versioning or migration, while old consumer instances still SADD into the exact same keys during a rolling deploy. During any rolling deploy, new-version zcard/zunionstore/zadd/zscan against keys holding old-version SADD data (and old-version sadd against new ZSET keys) fail with WRONGTYPE, so segments buffered before the deploy can never be merged or flushed and their spans are lost when the TTL expires.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type for the existing `span-buf:s:{...}:...` keyspace from SETs to ZSETs: `buffer.py` switches `sadd`->`zadd` and `sscan`->`zscan`, and the Lua script switches `scard/sunionstore`->`zcard/zunionstore` while using the same key format (`span-buf:s:{%s}:%s`). There is no key versioning, migration, or dual-read/write compatibility shown. During a rolling deploy, old instances will still write SETs into these keys while new code expects ZSETs (and vice versa), which in Redis yields `WRONGTYPE` errors for operations like `ZSCAN/ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE/ZADD` on SET keys or `SADD` on ZSET keys. That can prevent merging/flushing buffered segments until TTL expiry, causing span loss.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct indexing while every neighboring field uses `.get()`, because the ingest-spans schema permits spans without (or with null) precise end timestamps, e.g. from older Relay/producer versions. A span lacking the field raises KeyError inside process_batch (or feeds a None score into zadd at buffer.py:198, which redis rejects), poisoning and repeatedly failing the Kafka batch — the consumer stalls on spans the pre-diff code processed fine.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes `end_timestamp_precise` a required `Span` field and reads it via direct indexing in `process_batch` (`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]`). There is no fallback/default if the key is absent or null, and `buffer.py` now uses it as the Redis ZSET score (`zadd(... {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise})`), which would fail if `None`/missing. This introduces a clear failure mode (KeyError or Redis rejecting a non-numeric score) for any ingested span payloads that don’t include this field, causing batch processing to error repeatedly.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `enable_advanced` references `organization_context`, which is not defined anywhere in this endpoint's get() (not imported, not assigned in this method), and the expression evaluates unconditionally on every request rather than only when optimized_pagination=true is passed. Every non-superuser request to GET /api/0/organizations/<slug>/auditlogs/ raises NameError and returns a 500 (superusers short-circuit on is_superuser), taking down the audit-logs endpoint for all regular organization admins regardless of the query parameter.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new line `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` references `organization_context`, but this diff does not introduce any definition/import/assignment for `organization_context` in this method. Because this assignment executes before the `if use_optimized and enable_advanced:` branch, any non-superuser request will evaluate the right-hand side of the `or` and would raise `NameError` if `organization_context` is indeed undefined, independent of the `optimized_pagination` query param.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The advanced branch slices the queryset with a negative bound (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), but Django querysets do not support negative slice bounds — slicing compiles to SQL OFFSET, which raises — so the comment's claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any superuser who enables `optimized_pagination=true` with a cursor carrying a negative offset gets a 500: the sole advertised capability of OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot execute, and the promised 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds' is unreachable in any deployment.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the “advanced” path explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0` and then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django ORM does not support negative slice bounds for querysets (it compiles to OFFSET/LIMIT semantics and raises on negative indexing), so this code path will error if reached. The diff even adds comments claiming negative slicing is “properly handled automatically,” but the implementation relies on an unsupported behavior, making the advertised feature non-functional and potentially causing 500s for requests that supply a cursor with a negative offset.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a collage of DateTimePaginator method bodies (get_item_key, value_from_cursor, and the self.build_queryset call) grafted onto BasePaginator, which does not define build_queryset — BasePaginator's own get_result is pure offset slicing with no value-filtered queryset building — and its value_from_cursor returns the raw integer cursor value where a datetime is required. The first request through the optimized path raises AttributeError ('OptimizedCursorPaginator' object has no attribute 'build_queryset') before any query runs, so admins who set optimized_pagination=true get a 500 on every request and the feature is dead on arrival.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is added as `class OptimizedCursorPaginator(BasePaginator)` and its `get_result` calls `self.build_queryset(cursor_value, cursor.is_prev)`, but the new class does not define `build_queryset`. The PR also does not show any change adding `build_queryset` to `BasePaginator`. This makes it very likely that the optimized path in `organization_auditlogs.py` (`paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator` when `optimized_pagination=true`) will raise an `AttributeError` at runtime on the first request that hits this code path. Additionally, the new paginator’s `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unmodified, which is suspicious when the endpoint orders by a datetime field (`order_by="-datetime"`), but the missing `build_queryset` alone is sufficient to break the feature.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The endpoint forks into a second, parallel pagination implementation (OptimizedCursorPaginator, ~90 duplicated lines stitched from OffsetPaginator and DateTimePaginator) selected by an undocumented magic query-param string comparison (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus a role check, with no feature flag or options entry and no tests in the diff. One endpoint now serves two divergence-prone pagination contracts whose behavior differs by caller role; operators cannot disable the new path without a code deploy; and the duplicated paginator will drift from BasePaginator fixes, with breakage surfacing only as confusing admin-only 500s that non-admin reproduction cannot hit.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a second pagination path in `organization_auditlogs.get()` gated by a magic query param (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus a role check, switching from `DateTimePaginator` to a newly introduced `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with an extra kwarg (`enable_advanced_features=True`). There is no feature flag, settings toggle, or documented API option in the diff, and no tests were added for this new endpoint behavior. The new paginator class is a substantial bespoke implementation (~90 lines) that largely re-implements cursor/offset logic instead of reusing existing paginator logic, creating a concrete maintainability/divergence risk grounded in the added code and endpoint fork (even if the future “drift” consequences are speculative).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The eviction path silently truncates segments — zpopmin discards the oldest spans and publishes a partial segment with no metric or log — while this same PR deletes the flusher's only loud signal (the segment_span_count_exceeded metric and skip in buffer.py:446-452), so oversized segments now ship silently instead of failing observably. Operators lose the only means of detecting truncation; traces with >1000 spans are persisted as segments missing their earliest spans, so downstream segment processing computes from partial data; and when the root span's end_timestamp ranks among the oldest (clock skew / out-of-order ingestion), the has_root_span marker still fires and a rootless segment is published.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes segment overflow handling from “detect + loudly skip” to “silently truncate + continue.” In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, after merging via `zunionstore`, it enforces `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which drops the lowest-scored (oldest `end_timestamp_precise`) members with no metric/log path shown. In `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`, the prior overflow check that emitted `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and skipped the segment (deleted at old lines 446-452) is removed, and `_load_segment_data` now just extends payloads from `zscan` without any span-count guard. Net effect: oversized segments will be persisted/processed missing spans (data loss) with the previous observability signal removed, matching the finding’s core claim about silent truncation and loss of detection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The 1000-span cap is enforced only on the Lua insert path; process_spans writes into the same `span-buf:s:{...}` keys via `p.zadd` with no cap or eviction, and the flusher-side count guard was deleted, so the advertised bound is not a real invariant. Segments assembled through the Python tree path grow without limit in Redis (memory pressure on the shared cluster for hot traces) and exceed the intended cap with no remaining code path — insert-time or flush-time — able to notice or bound them.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a 1000-element cap only in `add-buffer.lua` via `zcard`/`zpopmin` on `set_key` (the `span-buf:s:{...}:...` ZSET). But the Python path `SpansBuffer.process_spans` now writes directly to the same key pattern with `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise ...})` and does not apply any cap/eviction. Additionally, in `_load_segment_data` the previous flush-time span-count guard (`if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ...`) was deleted, so oversized segments assembled via the Python tree path are no longer detected or bounded at flush time either. This makes the advertised 1000-span bound non-invariant and allows unbounded growth in Redis for those keys.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The eviction threshold is a hardcoded bare `1000` that replaces the existing configurable `self.max_segment_spans` — whose only reader this diff deletes from buffer.py — and the script now holds two same-valued `1000` literals with different units (redirect depth at line 30 vs span count here). Operators who configured max_segment_spans get silently ignored values (the option is now dead config), and the next editor can conflate the depth-1000 with the count-1000 or change one without the other, with no named constant tying the Lua cap to the Python option.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce hardcoded `1000` limits in `add-buffer.lua`: the redirect traversal loop is reduced to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and there is a new span-cap block `if span_count > 1000 then ... zpopmin(..., span_count - 1000) end`. In Python, the prior `self.max_segment_spans` enforcement in `_load_segment_data` is removed (the whole `segment_span_count_exceeded` branch is deleted), shifting span-count limiting into Lua with a fixed value. While the claim that `max_segment_spans` is now a “dead config” cannot be fully verified from this diff alone (it might be read elsewhere), the hardcoded constant replacing the prior configurable check and the presence of multiple unrelated `1000` literals is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/operability concern rather than a strictly provable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-walk bound is silently lowered from 10001 to 1001 iterations while the comment documenting the tradeoff ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') is deleted. Redirect chains between 1001 and 10000 deep now fall out of the loop with set_span_id pointing at a mid-chain node, so the following hset buffers subsequent spans under the wrong set id and the segment fragments never join — those fragments expire via TTL and their spans are lost, with the deleted comment hiding the known limitation.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` the redirect-walk loop bound is reduced from `for i = 0, 10000 do` (with an explicit comment about 10k-depth tradeoff) to `for i = 0, 1000 do` with no accompanying explanation. The loop updates `set_span_id` by following `hget` redirects and breaks only when the chain ends; if the chain is >1000 links, the loop will terminate due to the iteration limit with `set_span_id` still pointing to an intermediate node. Immediately after, the code does `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` and derives `set_key` from that `set_span_id`, so subsequent merges/write go to the wrong set id and deeper chains won’t converge as before. This is a behavior/correctness regression directly implied by the diff; the “silent” removal of the comment also matches the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The shared offset paginator's negative-offset handling is now internally inconsistent and contradicts its own comment: forward cursors silently clamp negative offsets to 0 (returning page one), while prev cursors pass the unclamped negative offset straight into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, which raises. Every endpoint using this base paginator now accepts forged/corrupted cursors with negative offsets either silently — returning the first page as if it were valid and masking cursor corruption — or with a 500 on the is_prev branch, instead of uniformly rejecting them as the pre-diff code did.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the shared offset-based paginator now does `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and then slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. This means a forged/corrupted cursor with a negative `offset` is silently clamped to 0 for forward pagination (returning the first page), but for `is_prev` the negative offset is passed through. Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indexes and will raise, producing a 500. Pre-diff, `queryset[offset:stop]` would consistently error for negative offsets regardless of direction, so the new behavior is internally inconsistent and introduces both masking of invalid cursors and a direction-dependent server error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] This audit-log pagination feature (hidden `optimized_pagination` query param, superuser/global-access gating, and the new OptimizedCursorPaginator) is an objective change unrelated to the PR's stated intent ('Optimize spans buffer insertion with eviction during insert'), smuggled into a Redis spans-buffer PR without acceptance from anyone reviewing audit-log API behavior. Role-dependent pagination semantics and a new undocumented query parameter with no feature flag or options entry ship under a PR whose reviewers accepted only span-buffer changes; regressions in this security-sensitive endpoint are unowned, cannot be disabled without a code revert, and cursor tokens minted by the admin-only paginator are fed back to DateTimePaginator when the param is dropped or the link is opened by a non-admin, breaking pagination continuity for audit-log users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff for a spans-buffer optimization PR also introduces a new audit-log API behavior change: `organization_auditlogs.py` adds a hidden `optimized_pagination=true` query param and role-based gating (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`) to switch paginator classes, plus it adds an entirely new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` in `sentry/api/paginator.py`. This is a nontrivial, security/UX-sensitive endpoint change that is unrelated in scope to the spans-buffer edits shown elsewhere in the diff. However, the specific claim that this *definitively* breaks pagination continuity when the param is dropped / non-admin opens the link is not directly verifiable from the diff alone (cursor compatibility depends on `paginate`/cursor encoding behavior not shown).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the queryset with a negative start (`results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` where `start_offset = cursor.offset < 0`), which raises Django's `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, directly contradicting the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any superuser/global-access request to the audit-logs endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` and a client-crafted cursor carrying a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses ints without rejecting negatives, as the cursors.py comment in this diff confirms) returns a 500 from an uncaught AssertionError instead of the promised bidirectional pagination; the unclamped prev-cursor else-branch at line 881 crashes the same way.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` that, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and slices a Django queryset with `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indexes (it asserts start/stop are non-negative), so this will raise an `AssertionError` rather than providing “negative offset” pagination as the inline comments claim. Additionally, even in the non-advanced branch, `start_offset = ... if not cursor.is_prev else offset` allows a negative `offset` when `cursor.is_prev` is true, leading to the same negative-slice crash.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] _load_segment_data now issues `p.zscan` against `span-buf:s:*` keys, but this diff changes those keys' Redis type from set to zset with no migration, so every key written by pre-deploy code (sadd/sunionstore) is still a SET with live TTL when the new flusher first runs. The first post-deploy flush cycle raises Redis WRONGTYPE on every still-live pre-deploy segment key, crashing the flush batch; retries keep failing until the TTL expires, so all segments buffered across the deploy window are silently lost.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data structure used for segment buffers at the same key names `span-buf:s:{...}:...` from SETs to ZSETs: `SpansBuffer.process_spans` switches `sadd` -> `zadd`, the Lua script switches `scard/sunionstore` -> `zcard/zunionstore`, and `_load_segment_data` switches `sscan` -> `zscan`. There is no compatibility handling or migration for pre-existing keys still holding SET values with an active TTL (`expire` remains in Lua). If any pre-deploy SET keys are still live when the new flusher runs, `p.zscan(key, ...)` will hit Redis WRONGTYPE, matching the finding’s described failure mode.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The script switches span-buf:s:* keys from set operations (scard/sunionstore) to zset operations (zcard/zunionstore) while buffer.py process_spans switches sadd to zadd on the same key names, with no key versioning, so old- and new-code consumers coexisting during a rolling deploy operate on the same keys with incompatible Redis types. During the deploy window every cross-version touch raises WRONGTYPE — old Lua `scard` on a zset written by new Python zadd, new Lua `zcard` on a set written by old code — so span insertion script calls error and incoming spans are dropped for the duration of mixed-version operation.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data type for the same key namespace `span-buf:s:{...}:<span_id>` from Sets to Sorted Sets without any key versioning/migration. In `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`, `process_spans` switches `sadd` to `zadd` on `span-buf:s:{...}:...`, and `_load_segment_data` switches `sscan` to `zscan`. In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the same keys are now read/merged using `zcard`/`zunionstore` and trimmed with `zpopmin`, whereas previously they were treated as sets (`scard`/`sunionstore`). Because the key names are unchanged, any mixed-version period (old code still doing set ops, new code doing zset ops) will hit Redis WRONGTYPE errors when either side touches a key written by the other, causing the Lua script to error and spans to be dropped during that window.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new eviction (`zpopmin` of the lowest end_timestamp_precise members whenever count > 1000) silently deletes spans that were accepted into the buffer — including segments well under the accepted max_segment_bytes budget — and the flusher then emits the remaining spans as a complete segment because has_root_span, the only completeness gate, is unaffected. Flushed segments are silently missing their earliest-ending spans with no marker, metric, or structural signal, so downstream segment assembly and trace views show truncated data indistinguishable from a complete segment — the buffer's accepted contract (skip oversized segments whole and loudly) is replaced by unmarked partial emission that no review accepted.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds silent span eviction in `add-buffer.lua`: after merging into the segment zset, it computes `span_count` and if `span_count > 1000` it runs `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`, dropping the lowest-score (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans with no metric/log/marker. At the same time, `buffer.py` removes the prior explicit oversize protection for span count (`max_segment_spans`) during load (`sscan`->`zscan` and deletes the block that skipped/errored when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`). Completeness gating shown here (`has_root_span_key` / `has_root_span`) is independent of span count and is not updated when eviction happens, so segments can flush as if complete while missing evicted spans. This is a real correctness/data-loss behavior introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch direct-indexes `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with no `.get` fallback for a field this diff itself introduces to the wire contract (the consumer test fixture adds the field only in this PR), making the consumer incompatible with in-flight messages produced by pre-deploy producers. During a rolling deploy, any Kafka message lacking the field raises KeyError inside process_batch, fails the batch, and turns the message into a poison pill the consumer retries indefinitely, stalling span ingestion on that partition.

adjudication.rationale: In `process_batch` (src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py) the code now does `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` after `rapidjson.loads`, with no `.get(...)`/default. This PR also adds `end_timestamp_precise` to the `Span` NamedTuple (src/sentry/spans/buffer.py) and updates tests to include the field, indicating it’s newly required by the consumer. If any consumed messages lack this key, the direct index will raise `KeyError` and break batch processing for those messages.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The eviction path drops buffered spans with no metrics.incr or logger call, breaking the buffer's established observability contract where every drop path (segment_size_exceeded, segment_span_count_exceeded) is instrumented. On-call engineers investigating incomplete segments or Redis memory pressure cannot distinguish evicted spans from lost ingestion, and the spans.buffer.flush_segments dashboards give no signal that the new dominant drop path ever fired.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new dominant drop/eviction path that silently removes spans without any metrics/logging. In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the new cap logic `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` evicts buffered spans. At the same time, the previous Python-side instrumentation for span-count drops in `_load_segment_data` (`metrics.incr("...segment_span_count_exceeded")` and `logger.error(...)`) was removed when switching from `sscan`/sets to `zscan`/sorted sets. There is no replacement `metrics.incr`/logger call tied to this eviction path in the diff, so observability for drops is reduced as the finding claims.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates the base paginator's get_result nearly verbatim, creating two hand-maintained copies of the cursor offset/extra/reversal math. The next fix to shared pagination math must be applied in both copies or the audit-log admin path silently diverges — this diff already modified the two copies differently (the base clamps via max(0, ...) in the same hunk while the copy adds the negative branch).

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` in `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` that re-implements the same offset/`extra`/prev-handling/reversal/cursor-building logic that already exists in the earlier `get_result` implementation (also modified in this diff). This creates two hand-maintained copies of pagination math. The two copies already diverge: the earlier `get_result` clamps `start_offset = max(0, offset)` when not `cursor.is_prev`, while `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` adds a special negative-offset branch when `enable_advanced_features` is set (`start_offset = cursor.offset`), otherwise falling back to the clamp logic. That duplication/divergence is a concrete maintainability/architecture concern introduced by the change, not a directly verifiable runtime defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] `organization_context` is never defined in OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get (this diff adds no definition or import for it), so evaluating `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises NameError. Every audit-log GET by a non-superuser — the endpoint's entire audience of org owners/admins, since only `request.user.is_superuser == True` short-circuits past the expression — returns a raw 500, fully breaking the organization audit-logs API.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new logic sets `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but this diff does not show any definition or import of `organization_context` in the method/hunk. If `organization_context` is not defined earlier in `get`, then for any non-superuser the `or` expression will evaluate the second operand and raise `NameError`, causing a 500. The defect is that the diff introduces a new identifier reference without any visible binding in this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] process_batch reads `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct key indexing on a field that pre-existing ingest-spans messages do not carry (the same payload's other optional fields, parent_span_id/is_remote, are read with .get, and sentry's Kafka topics have no schema enforcement on retained messages). Any message produced before the field was emitted (old SDK protocol payloads, retained topic contents, not-yet-upgraded producers during rollout) raises KeyError inside the arroyo RunTask; the batch's offsets never commit and the consumer crash-loops on the poisoned batch, halting span ingestion for the partition.

adjudication.rationale: In `process_batch` the new `Span` field `end_timestamp_precise` is populated via direct indexing (`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]`) after `val = rapidjson.loads(payload.value)` (cast only affects typing). Unlike other potentially-missing fields (`parent_span_id`, `is_remote`) which use `.get`, this will raise `KeyError` for any message payload that lacks `end_timestamp_precise`. The diff shows no fallback/default handling, so ingestion can break on older/partial payloads.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The span-buf keys change from Redis SETs to ZSETs (zcard/zunionstore here, zadd in buffer.py's process_spans, zscan in the flusher) with no key versioning or type conversion, so every one of these operations raises WRONGTYPE on any key written as a set by the pre-deploy code. The buffer keys persist in Redis across the deploy window under their TTLs, so during rollout the new consumer hits WRONGTYPE on stale keys, the Lua script returns an error to process_batch, and span ingestion halt-loops until old keys expire — old and new consumers cannot coexist.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data structure for the same `span-buf:s:{...}:...` keys from SET to ZSET: `buffer.py` switches `sadd` -> `zadd`, flusher switches `sscan` -> `zscan`, and the Lua script switches `scard/sunionstore` -> `zcard/zunionstore` on existing keys. There is no key versioning (same key format is used) and no type-checking/conversion logic in the diff. During a rollout, pre-existing keys written as SETs (with TTL) would cause the new ZSET operations (e.g., `zcard`, `zscan`, `zunionstore`, `zadd`) to raise Redis WRONGTYPE errors, and likewise old code would fail against new ZSET keys. This is a concrete, diff-grounded backward/forward compatibility defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The zpopmin eviction silently deletes the earliest-timestamped span payloads whenever a buffered segment exceeds 1000 members, and the segment is still flushed downstream as if complete. Traces with more than 1000 buffered spans produce segments with silently missing children (wrong derived end timestamp/exclusive time, incomplete trace view), and the diff simultaneously deletes the flusher's segment_span_count_exceeded metric and error log in buffer.py — the only prior observability — so this data loss is invisible to operators and users.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a hard cap in `add-buffer.lua` that truncates sorted sets: after merging with `zunionstore`, it computes `span_count` and if `span_count > 1000` executes `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`, which permanently deletes the lowest-score members (scores are `end_timestamp_precise` per `buffer.py` `zadd`, so these are the earliest end timestamps). There is no signaling that truncation occurred, and `buffer.py` also removes the prior span-count guard/observability (`segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and `logger.error` block were deleted in `_load_segment_data`), so oversized segments will be flushed with missing spans without operator visibility. This is concrete data loss / incorrect trace reconstruction introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key passes the row's `datetime` attribute (a datetime instance, since the only endpoint wired to this class paginates order_by="-datetime" on AuditLogEntry) directly into math.floor(), which raises TypeError because datetime defines no __float__/__floor__. Every `optimized_pagination=true` audit-logs request that yields a full page crashes inside build_cursor when it computes the boundary cursor key and returns a raw 500 instead of a paginated result — the advertised optimized path cannot serve a single page.

adjudication.rationale: In the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, `get_item_key()` does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then passes that `value` through `math.floor/ceil` (casts to `int`). In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the only wired usage orders audit log entries by `order_by="-datetime"`. That implies the cursor key will be the `datetime` field on each row, i.e. a `datetime` object, which is not compatible with `math.floor/ceil` and would raise `TypeError`. This would break the optimized pagination path at runtime when building cursors over audit log results.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The advertised negative-offset branch passes `cursor.offset` raw into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`, and Django querysets reject negative slice bounds before generating SQL (an SQL OFFSET cannot be negative) — the inline comment claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false. A superuser paging with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor carrying a negative offset — the exact input this branch exists to serve — gets an unhandled exception and a raw 500 instead of the bidirectional page the feature promises.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the new “negative offset” path explicitly sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0` and then does `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (see `if self.enable_advanced_features and cursor.offset < 0:`). Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices (it raises before SQL generation because SQL OFFSET cannot be negative). This makes the advertised feature (`optimized_pagination=true` + `enable_advanced_features=True`) prone to an unhandled exception/500 when a cursor with a negative offset is used, contradicting the inline comment that negative slicing is “properly handled automatically.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rewritten OffsetPaginator slicing converts a forward cursor with a negative offset from an error into silent success (max(0, offset) rewrites the request to offset 0 and serves the first page with 200), while the is_prev branch still forwards the raw negative offset into the queryset slice, which the ORM rejects. Any client of every OffsetPaginator-backed endpoint sending a crafted/malformed negative-offset cursor (cursors are unvalidated user-supplied base64) now gets either a 200 serving the wrong page as if the requested position were honored — hiding the bug the previous 500 exposed — or an unhandled 500 with is_prev; neither branch implements the bidirectional pagination the comment claims.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the `OffsetPaginator.get_result` slice was changed from `queryset[offset:stop]` to `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` and then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. This means a malformed/user-supplied cursor with a negative `offset` and `is_prev == False` is silently rewritten to `0` and returns the first page (wrong position) instead of erroring. Meanwhile when `cursor.is_prev` is true, the raw (possibly negative) `offset` is still used as the slice start, which Django ORM slicing does not support (negative slicing raises), causing an unhandled 500. The diff also shows no validation of cursor offsets (Cursor stores `self.offset = int(offset)`), so the inconsistent behavior is reachable via crafted cursors, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Deleting the max_segment_spans check removes the only enforcement site for self.max_segment_spans — the segment-span cap now exists solely as a hard-coded 1000 inside add-buffer.lua. adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the only visible enforcement of `self.max_segment_spans` in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` (the `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ...` block is deleted). In its place, truncation is now enforced in `add-buffer.lua` via a hard-coded `1000` cap (`if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end`). Nothing in the diff ties that `1000` to `self.max_segment_spans`, so any operator tuning of `max_segment_spans` would no longer affect the effective limit, which is a behavior/config regression introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The redirect-hop bound is cut from 10000 to 1000 while the comment documenting the correctness contract ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") is deleted, hiding the failure mode it explained. Redirect chains deeper than 1000 hops now resolve to an intermediate span's set and strand there — that intermediate span's script invocation has already run, so nothing re-merges them upward — and the payloads silently drop out of the true segment when the key expires; the documented support bound regresses 10x with no error or metric.

adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua` the redirect-chase loop bound is reduced from `0..10000` to `0..1000` and the prior comment describing the correctness limitation is removed. The loop only updates `set_span_id` while it finds redirects; if a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop will terminate without hitting the `break`, leaving `set_span_id` pointing at whatever redirect was reached at hop 1000 rather than the true terminal/root. The script then persists `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)` and unions spans into `set_key` derived from that intermediate `set_span_id`, meaning deep chains can be split across multiple sets and never merged by this invocation. This is a concrete behavioral regression visible in the diff (reduced supported depth with no error/metric), and can lead to incorrect segment joining for deep redirect chains.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The endpoint's pagination implementation silently switches on an undocumented query param combined with the caller's role, with no feature flag or options entry gating the new path. The same audit-log request now runs two different paginators depending on who sends it, so pagination defects on the new path reproduce only for privileged users and are invisible when ordinary org admins and support try to reproduce reports; operators cannot disable the new path without a code deploy.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, pagination behavior now depends on an undocumented query param (`optimized_pagination=true`) and caller role (`request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`). When both are true it switches paginator class to `OptimizedCursorPaginator` and passes `enable_advanced_features=True`; otherwise it uses `DateTimePaginator`. The diff shows no feature flag, no options/config gating, and no API surface documentation/response metadata indicating the alternate path, so the same request can exercise two different pagination implementations depending on who calls it, making privileged-only pagination issues harder to reproduce and leaving no runtime kill switch besides code changes.
